title: Tax Deduction or Collection at Source and Advance Tax
outcomes: Explain how tax is recovered during the year and compute TDS on salary.
Identify the Table row, rate and threshold for common payments to residents and any person.
Apply TCS and the higher rates for missing PAN.
Compute advance tax instalments and interest under sections 398, 424 and 425.

meta.exam_tip: For every payment, write the row, payer status, payee status, rate and threshold before computing. For advance tax, always work cumulatively.

concepts.title: How tax is recovered during the year (ss. 390-391) and TDS on salary (s. 392)
body: Section 390: during the tax year the Government recovers tax in three ways — deduction or collection at source, advance tax, and tax an employer pays on non-monetary perquisites under section 392(2)(a). Tax so paid is credited to the person whose income it relates to.

Section 391: where nothing is deducted (no provision, or a failure to deduct), the payee pays directly. A deductor who neither deducts nor pays, where the payee has also not paid, is treated as an assessee-in-default.

Section 392(1): when salary is paid, the employer withholds tax using the average rate of tax on the employee's estimated income. The employee tells the employer each year which regime he intends to use; if he says nothing, the default regime of section 202(1) is assumed.

An employer may choose to bear tax on non-monetary perquisites at the same average rate; that tax is exempt for the employee but not deductible for the employer. Section 392(7): trustees deduct 10% from a taxable premature PF withdrawal of ₹50,000 or more.
concepts.analogy: TDS on salary spreads the year's tax evenly over pay days, based on the employer's best estimate.
concepts.work: Salary ₹8,50,000 with tax of ₹75,400 gives an average rate of about 9.4%, applied to each payment.

concepts.title: TDS on payments to residents (s. 393(1))
body: Section 393(1) lists payments to residents. Unless stated otherwise, tax is deducted on the whole amount once the threshold is crossed, at the earlier of credit (including a suspense account) and payment.

Key rows: insurance commission (2%, or 10% for a domestic company payee; ₹20,000); other commission or brokerage (2%; ₹20,000); rent by individuals/HUFs outside the turnover test (2%; ₹50,000 a month); rent by specified persons (2% plant and machinery, 10% land, building or furniture; ₹50,000 a month); transfer of non-agricultural immovable property (1% of the higher of consideration and stamp duty value; ₹50 lakh); compulsory acquisition (10%; ₹5 lakh).

Further rows: units of mutual funds (10%; ₹10,000); interest from banks and notified post-office deposits (10%; ₹1,00,000 for senior citizens, ₹50,000 others) and from other specified persons (₹10,000); contract work (1% individual/HUF, 2% others; ₹30,000 single or ₹1,00,000 a year); work, professional fees or commission paid by individuals/HUFs not otherwise covered (2%; ₹50 lakh); professional and technical fees, royalty and non-compete fees (10%, or 2% for technical services and film royalty; ₹50,000 each; nil limit for directors' fees); dividend (10%); life policy proceeds (2% of the income part; ₹1,00,000); purchase of goods by a buyer with turnover above ₹10 crore (0.1% of the amount above ₹50 lakh); business perquisites (10%; ₹20,000).

A "specified person" is anyone other than an individual or HUF, or an individual/HUF whose turnover in the preceding year exceeded ₹1 crore (business) or ₹50 lakh (profession). Individuals deducting on rent, property purchase and the ₹50-lakh contract row need no TAN.
concepts.analogy: Think of the Table as a menu: find the row, then check payer, payee, rate and limit — in that order.
concepts.work: A small shopkeeper with ₹60 lakh turnover paying ₹25,000 brokerage deducts nothing; a company paying the same must deduct 2%.

concepts.title: TDS on payments to any person (s. 393(3)) and the PAN rule (s. 397)
body: Section 393(3) covers payments to any person, resident or not: winnings from lotteries, crosswords, card games and betting (30%; above ₹10,000 per transaction); online game winnings (30%, on net winnings at withdrawal or year end, no threshold); horse-race winnings (30%; ₹10,000); lottery ticket commission (2%; ₹20,000); cash withdrawals from banks (2% above ₹1 crore, or ₹3 crore for co-operative societies); and partner's salary, commission, bonus or interest paid by a firm (10%; ₹20,000).

Section 397(2): a payee who does not furnish a valid PAN suffers TDS at the highest of the specified rate, the rate in force and 20% (5% for the purchase-of-goods row). For rent by individuals, this higher deduction is still capped at the last month's rent. Where the normal rate already exceeds 20%, as for winnings at 30%, nothing changes.
For TCS without PAN the rate is the higher of twice the normal rate and 5%, but not above 20%.
concepts.analogy: Missing PAN is expensive: the law pushes the rate up so that the payee has every reason to give it.
concepts.work: A machinery lessor without PAN suffers 20% instead of 2% on rent.

concepts.title: Tax collection at source (s. 394)
body: Section 394 makes certain sellers and others collect tax from the buyer at the time of debit or receipt, whichever is earlier.

Sale of alcoholic liquor, tendu leaves, forest produce, scrap and coal, lignite or iron ore, and grant of a parking lot, toll plaza, mine or quarry: 2% for minerals and others as per the Table. Buyers who use such goods for manufacture or power (not trading) can give a declaration to avoid collection.

Motor vehicles and notified goods above ₹10 lakh: 1%. Remittances under the Liberalised Remittance Scheme above ₹10 lakh: 2% for education or medical treatment, 20% for other purposes, on the excess over ₹10 lakh; overseas tour packages: 2% up to ₹10 lakh and 20% above.
concepts.analogy: TCS works like TDS in reverse — the seller adds the tax to the bill and passes it on to the Government.
concepts.work: A student remitting ₹13 lakh for foreign tuition suffers TCS of 2% on ₹3 lakh, i.e. ₹6,000.

concepts.title: Defaults: interest and assessee-in-default (s. 398)
body: Section 398: a person who fails to deduct or collect, or after doing so fails to pay, is treated as an assessee-in-default for that tax.

Interest is simple: 1% a month or part of a month from the date tax was deductible or collectible to the date it is actually deducted or collected; 1.5% a month or part of a month from the date of deduction or collection to the date of payment. It must be paid before the quarterly statement is filed.

Relief: if the payee has filed his return, included the income and paid the tax on it, and an accountant certifies this, the payer is not treated as in default; interest at 1% then runs only until the payee's return date. Unpaid tax collected or deducted, with interest, is a charge on all the payer's assets.
concepts.analogy: Late deduction costs 1% a month; holding the Government's money costs 1.5% a month.
concepts.work: Tax deducted on 10 May but paid on 20 July attracts 1.5% × 3 months.

concepts.title: Advance tax (ss. 403-410) and interest (ss. 424-425)
body: Sections 403–404: advance tax is paid during the financial year on the current year's income when the tax payable (after TDS/TCS) is ₹10,000 or more. A resident individual aged 60 or more with no business or professional income is exempt.

Section 408: instalments by 15 June (15%), 15 September (45%), 15 December (75%) and 15 March (100%), cumulatively. Presumptive-income taxpayers under section 58(2) pay the whole by 15 March. Payment up to 31 March still counts as advance tax for that year.

Section 424: if advance tax paid is less than 90% of assessed tax, simple interest at 1% a month runs from 1 April after the tax year on the shortfall until the date of determination of income (reduced for self-assessment tax paid).

Section 425: for deferment, 3% (three months at 1%) on each shortfall at 15 June, 15 September and 15 December, and 1% at 15 March. No interest arises on the first two dates if at least 12% and 36% respectively were paid.
concepts.analogy: Advance tax means "pay as you earn" for income that has no deductor watching it.
concepts.work: If 13% of the year's tax is paid by 15 June, no section 425 interest arises for June.

illustrations.title: A salaried tenant as deductor
illustrations.q: Ms. Kavya, a salaried employee with no business income, rents a flat from Mr. Rohan at ₹60,000 a month from 1 July 2026 and stays on beyond March 2027. Is TDS required? If so, when and how much? What if Mr. Rohan does not give his PAN?

Answer
rows: Section 393(1) [Table: Sl. No. 2(i)] — an individual who is not a specified person paying rent above ₹50,000 a month
Once, from the rent for March 2027 (the last month of the tax year)
20% gives ₹1,08,000, but the deduction cannot go beyond one month's rent: 60,000

checks.label: TDS without PAN, capped at last month's rent

illustrations.title: Small bills that add up
illustrations.q: Nimbus Ltd. paid a firm of painters for four separate jobs in tax year 2026-27: ₹25,000, ₹28,000, ₹30,000 and ₹22,000 (the last in February 2027). No single bill crossed ₹30,000. Is TDS needed and how much?

Working

jobs.title: Vendor master review
jobs.situation: An accounts head asks which new vendor payments need TDS.
steps: Classify each vendor by nature of payment and Table row.
Check whether the company is a "specified" or "designated" person.
Track single and yearly thresholds in the ERP.
Collect PAN before the first payment.
jobs.takeaway: Most TDS errors come from the wrong row or a missing PAN, not from arithmetic.

jobs.title: Advance tax reminder
jobs.situation: A consultant with rising fee income asks how much to pay by 15 December.
steps: Estimate the year's income and tax.
Pay up to 75% of the balance, net of earlier instalments.
jobs.takeaway: A quarterly re-estimate avoids most section 425 interest.

mcqs.q: If an employee does not tell the employer which tax regime he intends to use, the employer deducts tax:
options: Under the default regime of section 202(1)
mcqs.explain: The law presumes the employee stays in the default regime when no intimation is given, and the employer computes TDS on that basis. In practice: collect the declaration in April.
mcqs.topic: How tax is recovered during the year (ss. 390-391) and TDS on salary (s. 392)

mcqs.q: Rent of ₹55,000 a month paid by a private company for an office building attracts TDS at:
mcqs.explain: A company is a specified person; for land, building, furniture or fittings the rate is 10%, while plant and machinery attract 2%. In practice: split composite rent if the agreement shows both.

mcqs.q: A flat is bought for ₹48 lakh but its stamp duty value is ₹52 lakh. TDS by the buyer:
mcqs.explain: TDS applies when either consideration or stamp duty value is ₹50 lakh or more, at 1% of the higher figure: 1% of ₹52 lakh = ₹52,000. In practice: the buyer needs no TAN.

mcqs.q: A bank pays FD interest of ₹70,000 in the year to a resident aged 66. TDS:
mcqs.explain: For senior citizens, banks deduct only when interest exceeds ₹1,00,000 in the year; ₹70,000 is below that, so nothing is deducted. In practice: the limit is ₹50,000 for others.

mcqs.q: A company with turnover of ₹40 crore buys goods worth ₹80 lakh from one seller in the year. TDS:
mcqs.explain: The buyer deducts 0.1% only on the amount above ₹50 lakh: 0.1% × ₹30 lakh = ₹3,000. In practice: track purchases per seller.

mcqs.q: A firm pays a partner interest on capital of ₹25,000 during the year. TDS:
mcqs.explain: Section 393(3) requires a firm to deduct 10% on salary, remuneration, commission, bonus or interest to a partner when the yearly total exceeds ₹20,000, and then on the whole amount. In practice: interest credited to capital account counts.
mcqs.topic: TDS on payments to any person (s. 393(3)) and the PAN rule (s. 397)

mcqs.q: A machinery lessor gives no PAN. TDS on ₹1,00,000 monthly lease rent by a company is at:
mcqs.explain: The rate becomes the highest of the normal 2%, the rate in force and 20%, so 20% applies. In practice: ask for PAN before the first credit.
mcqs.topic: TDS on payments to any person (s. 393(3)) and the PAN rule (s. 397)

mcqs.q: TCS on an LRS remittance of ₹15 lakh for a holiday (not a tour package) is:
mcqs.explain: For purposes other than education or medical treatment, 20% applies to the amount above ₹10 lakh: 20% × ₹5 lakh = ₹1,00,000. In practice: the bank collects it at the time of remittance.

mcqs.q: Tax deducted on 5 June is paid to the Government on 12 August. Interest under section 398:
mcqs.explain: After deduction, delay in payment attracts 1.5% for every month or part of a month. 5 June to 12 August covers parts of three months. In practice: remit by the due date.

mcqs.q: Advance tax is NOT payable by:
options: A resident aged 70 with only pension and interest income
A doctor aged 62 with professional income
mcqs.explain: A resident individual aged 60 or more without income from business or profession is exempt. The doctor has professional income, and the others owe ₹10,000 or more. In practice: such seniors pay self-assessment tax instead.

mcqs.q: By 15 September, a non-presumptive taxpayer must have paid, cumulatively:
mcqs.explain: The schedule is 15%, 45%, 75% and 100% by June, September, December and March. Paying at least 36% by September avoids section 425 interest for that date. In practice: compute cumulatively.

mcqs.q: Section 424 interest applies when advance tax paid is less than what share of assessed tax?
mcqs.explain: Interest at 1% a month from 1 April after the tax year arises only if advance tax falls below 90% of assessed tax, and is then charged on the shortfall. In practice: assessed tax is after TDS and relief.

summary: Recovery during the year: TDS/TCS, advance tax, employer-paid perquisite tax (s. 390).
Salary: average rate on estimated income (s. 392).
s. 393(1): residents; s. 393(3): any person; s. 394: TCS.
No PAN: TDS at least 20% (5% for goods); TCS higher of 2× and 5%, max 20%.
remember: Rent cap: higher TDS cannot exceed last month's rent for individuals.
Seniors 60+ without business income pay no advance tax.
traps: Purchase of goods TDS only on the excess over ₹50 lakh.

viva.q: At what rate does an employer deduct tax from salary?
viva.model: At the average rate of income-tax, worked out on the employee's estimated income for the year under the regime he has intimated, and applied at each payment.

viva.q: Who is a specified person for TDS on commission or interest?
viva.model: Any person other than an individual or HUF, and an individual or HUF whose turnover in the preceding year was above ₹1 crore for a business or ₹50 lakh for a profession.

viva.q: What happens if the payee does not furnish PAN?
viva.model: Tax is deducted at the highest of the specified rate, the rate in force and 20%, and collected at the higher of twice the rate and 5% capped at 20%.

viva.q: What interest applies for late deposit of TDS?
viva.model: Simple interest of 1.5% for every month or part of a month from the date of deduction to the date of payment, and 1% a month for late deduction.

viva.q: When does advance tax become payable?
viva.model: When the tax payable for the year after TDS and TCS is ₹10,000 or more, in four cumulative instalments by 15 June, 15 September, 15 December and 15 March.

cases.title: Mehta Traders' year-end
cases.case: Mehta Traders, a partnership firm with last year's turnover of ₹14 crore, made these payments in tax year 2026-27: legal fees to a resident advocate ₹45,000 and ₹20,000 (two matters); rent for a warehouse ₹70,000 a month; interest on capital to partner Ravi ₹60,000; and goods purchased from Leela Mills ₹1.1 crore. All payees have given PAN.

mcqs.explain: Professional fees above ₹50,000 in the year attract 10% on the whole amount; ₹65,000 in total gives ₹6,500. In practice: aggregate all matters for the same payee.

mcqs.q: Monthly TDS on the warehouse rent:
mcqs.explain: A firm is a specified person and a warehouse is a building, so 10% applies to ₹70,000 a month. In practice: deduct at credit or payment, whichever is earlier.

mcqs.q: TDS on Ravi's interest on capital:
mcqs.explain: A firm deducts 10% on interest to a partner once the year's total exceeds ₹20,000: 10% × ₹60,000 = ₹6,000. In practice: credit to capital account also triggers TDS.
mcqs.topic: TDS on payments to any person (s. 393(3)) and the PAN rule (s. 397)

mcqs.q: TDS on purchases from Leela Mills:
mcqs.explain: The firm's turnover is above ₹10 crore, so it deducts 0.1% on purchases above ₹50 lakh: 0.1% × ₹60 lakh = ₹6,000. In practice: TDS takes priority over the seller's TCS.
